title: Longest Increasing Path In a Matrix
statement: You get a grid of numbers. A path moves up, down, left or right, and every step must land on a strictly bigger number. You may start anywhere and cannot move diagonally. Return how many cells the longest such path visits.

example.caption: Starting at the 1 you can climb 1, 2, 6, 9. That is 4 cells, and no path is longer.

idea.sentence: The longest path starting at a cell is 1 plus the best of its bigger neighbours, so store that answer in a memo table the first time and the recursion never repeats work.

jargon.plain: Remember each answer the first time you compute it. A later call for the same cell reads the table instead of recursing again.
Greater than, not equal. Equal neighbours are never part of a path, so the path cannot loop.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a matrix (list of equal-length rows). Keep it to 2 by 3 or 2 by 2, each cell takes two steps.

vars.meaning: number of cells, r times c

compare.bruteLabel: Walk every path from every cell
compare.unit: cell visits (brute force really grows as 3 to the power of the path length, drawn as the closest shape)

rows.name: Plain DFS
rows.note: Every cell starts its own search and the same cells are walked again and again by different paths.

rows.name: DFS with memo
rows.note: Each cell is solved once and looks at 4 neighbours. The memo and the recursion stack are both at most n deep.

fast.takeaway: The memo is the DP table: one cell per grid cell. Strictly increasing steps mean there is no cycle, so the recursion always ends and the fill order is decided by the recursion itself.

stages.title: Memo table
stages.note: Make a table the size of the grid. memo[r][c] is the longest path starting at that cell. 0 means not computed.

stages.title: Memo hit
stages.note: If the cell already holds a number, return it. No walking, no recursion.

stages.title: Go uphill
stages.note: A new cell asks each strictly bigger neighbour for its longest path.

stages.title: Fill on return
stages.note: When all neighbours have answered, store 1 plus the best answer in the memo.

stages.title: Try every start
stages.note: Call the search from every cell, keep the largest answer. Repeats are memo hits.

edges.title: All numbers equal
edges.why: No neighbour is strictly bigger, so every cell is a path of length 1. Using at-least-equal would loop forever.

edges.title: Empty matrix
edges.why: There is no start cell. Check rows before reading the first row for the column count.

edges.title: One long row
edges.why: A single chain. The recursion goes ten deep from the first cell, and every later start is a memo hit.

edges.title: Negative numbers
edges.why: Only the order of values matters. The memo holds path lengths, never cell values, so 0 still safely means not computed.

gotchas.text: 0 in the memo means not computed, which is safe because a real answer is at least 1. If you used a memo that can hold a real 0, use -1 or a separate seen table.
The step must be strictly bigger. With equal allowed, two neighbours could call each other forever. Strictness is also why no visited set is needed.
Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0)) gives each row its own array. new Array(rows).fill([]) would share one row.
make([][]int, rows) has nil rows. Allocate each row. A recursive closure must be declared first with var dfs func(r, c int) int, then assigned, so it can call itself.
Recursion depth can reach the number of cells for a snake-shaped matrix. That is fine for small grids. For huge ones, sort cells by value and fill in that order, or use a topological order.

recap.pattern: DFS with memo on a grid
recap.key: memo[r][c] = 1 + max(memo of strictly bigger neighbours). Fill it by recursion and return the stored value on a repeat.
moves: Make a memo table of 0s the size of the grid
dfs(r,c): if memo is set, return it
Otherwise 1 + best of the strictly bigger neighbours, store it
Run dfs from every cell and keep the max
